scenario: AITA for telling my teacher 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!' | 20, almost 21, f. taking my first semester of uni since i can finally afford it. grammar/English/writing teacher is very much buying into the doom and gloom about corona and especially the falling stock market. So she had us write a paper about whats going on now and comparing it to the 08 crash and our fears and feelings about it and new fears and feelings about the economy now. Thing is... 08 and 09 were AWESOME for me. My little 9ish year old self had a fun couple of years. Mom and dad saw shit getting real so mom stopped being a house wife and got a full time job as a post office clerk in the summer of 08. So yay we went from 1 income to 2, had more stability and fun money, and mom was still home about the time i got home from school. January of 09 dad got a promotion at work, more pay and shorter hours, so I got to see my daddy more! And again the household income went up. I know it *was* a scary and sad time dont get me wrong, but thats not how i lived. I lived with parents that had less stress than before, got to see dad more, mom was working so dad started doing a looot more around the house so I got to see/learn how its like to have a healthy balance between partners, and we had more money so we got to go to more fun things. Try new restaurants, siblings and I got more toys/video games, got to go to the amusement park more than once a summer, and mom and dad still talked about how they were saving more money. So yeah... good times. Now, well my fiance just got his masters degree in CS, and a promotion at his job due to it, and is helping me through uni with money to spare. Yeah, you can see where this is going. Things are headed up again. So thats what I put in my paper. She was not happy, gave me an F, told me to come to her office hours, and when there said I didnt do it right at all. She said she wanted my fears and worries not for me to brag about how great life is for me and me alone. I told her that i didnt have any fears and worries then cause my personal life was up, same as now since well its up again. she tried to berate me some more about honesty and accountability in writing, when i stopped her and told her 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!'. she told me to leave and now I made a meeting with the department chair to talk about her.

Tone & Respect (or Lack Thereof)** - Your response ("*what more do you want bitch?!*") is **disrespectful, aggressive, and unprofessional**. Even if you were upset, calling a teacher a derogatory term (especially in an academic setting) is a **major breach of decorum**. Teachers expect students to engage critically but with **civility**. Your outburst undermines the very discussion you were having. - **Professionalism matters in academia**—even in heated moments, you’re expected to regulate your emotions. This could reflect poorly on you in future interactions with faculty, advisors, or employers. ### **2. The Core Issue: Misaligned Expectations** Your teacher’s feedback wasn’t *wrong*—she wanted a **critical, reflective analysis**, not a **personal victory lap**. Your paper framed the 2008 crash as a *positive* experience for you, which might not align with the **historical, economic, or societal context** of the assignment. - **Possible fixes for next time**: - Acknowledge the broader impact of the crash (e.g., "While my family benefited, others faced hardship..."). - Tie your personal experience to **economic themes** (e.g., "My family’s stability contrasts with the broader recession’s effects..."). - If you *genuinely* have no fears, say so—but frame it as part of a larger discussion (e.g., "My personal situation is secure, but I recognize systemic vulnerabilities..."). ### **3. The Department Chair Meeting** You’re right to escalate—**this is a serious issue**. However, your approach to the meeting should focus on: - **Clarifying expectations** (e.g., "I felt my paper was honest but didn’t meet the assignment’s critical analysis requirement"). - **Requesting a grade review** (e.g., "I’d like to revise and resubmit with adjustments"). - **Avoiding defensiveness**—your teacher’s reaction was harsh, but your response escalated the conflict. ### **4. Long-Term Consequences** - **Academic reputation**: Professors talk. If this becomes known, it could affect future recommendations, internships, or research opportunities. - **Emotional fallout**: While your anger is valid, this kind of outburst can leave lasting resentment. It’s better to channel frustration into **constructive advocacy** (e.g., writing a revised paper, seeking mediation). --- ### **What You Could Have Done Instead** 1. **Stayed calm in the moment**: - *"I understand the assignment’s focus on fears, but my experience was positive. Could we discuss how to incorporate that into a critical analysis?"* 2. **Revised the paper** (if allowed) to meet expectations while keeping your perspective. 3. **Framed the meeting with the chair as a solution, not a confrontation**: - *"I’d like to address the grade discrepancy and ensure future assignments align with my understanding of expectations."* --- ### **Final Thought** Your story is **valid**—your family’s resilience during 2008 is a real, positive experience. But **academic writing isn’t about personal bragging**; it’s about **engaging with ideas critically**. Your teacher’s reaction was over-the-top, but your response made it worse. **Next time**, channel your confidence into **persuasive, well-structured arguments**—not verbal outbursts.
